I am disappointed in the comments (except you brother_tempus, you always make me smile):

Consider: someone earning $7.25/hour for 40 hours/week earns a gross of $15,080/year. Same calculation at $15.00/hour equals $31,200 annually. A raise in the minimum, would remove a large number of marginally employed persons from food stamps and welfare.

The current federal minimum wage level was adjusted to $7.25/hour in 2009. Adjusting for inflation since then, the equivalent number is at least $15.00/hour (with some calculations as high as $26.16/per hour).

Yes, there are quite a few "mom&pop" businesses that will not be able to pay a living wage. I would argue that these businesses need to reassess their business strategy and either increase sales or lower all costs (profit margins will take a hit in these examples of business that are not able to adapt) To me, this is a good thing. Businesses need to adapt, need to innovate to stay competitive and successful.

Employers that take advantage of the current low minimum wage level (Wal-Mart and McDonalds are prime examples) actually assist their employees in applying for food stamps and welfare benefits. In essence, a low wage provides a government subsidy to those employers. By raising the minimum wage to a living wage, people without skills will have resources to get training, actually have less pressure to ever borrow money at exorbitant interest rates (pay day loans).

I think that the full repercussions of stepping up the minimum wage to approximate what inflation would have adjusted it to will cause reductions in employment (wouldn't it be nice to see most of those payday loan places close shop - and some government programs will need fewer personnel).

Businesses that can adapt will survive (and may actually improve). More money in the economy will increase spending in automobiles and housing. Where is the downside?

wouldn't it be better to figure out why some expenses are so high and lower them? Rent, mortgage, food, Insurance, tuition, cars, fuel, etc. Lots of this stuff is only expensive because of un-regulated greed. A little restraint here would be nice.

Historically speaking, paying high wage for low skilled work was what essentially led to the middle class (Henry ford did this), now the middle class is small, and 15 really isn't a lot of money these days. The problem is more that the manufacturing job market, the IT professional market (and several others) have been largely off shored.
